passage:
Monday: Gurleen's first week at the Berlin office. Her team lead, Siddharth, raised a problem with her report bluntly in the meeting. She went home feeling humiliated and cried on the phone to her mother.

Thursday: Over coffee, Siddharth, who had grown up in Delhi and worked in Germany for six years, explained that here people often said problems directly and it wasn't personal. "It took me a year," he admitted. Gurleen wasn't sure she believed him.

Three weeks later: A German colleague, Jonas, told her flatly her slides were confusing. Gurleen breathed, said thanks, and asked which slide. He showed her, then added, "The data is very good." She noticed she didn't need him to soften it. She also noticed she still preferred to be gentle herself, and that was fine.

qa.q: Who explained that direct feedback wasn't personal?
qa.a: Siddharth, her team lead, explained it over coffee.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel after the first meeting, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt humiliated; she cried on the phone to her mother that evening.

qa.q: What helped Gurleen adapt over those weeks?
qa.a: Understanding the local style from someone who had adjusted himself, and practising asking specific questions instead of taking it personally.

qa.q: How might Jonas see Gurleen's response to his feedback?
qa.a: He likely saw her as open and professional, since she thanked him and asked which slide.

grounding: Shows a young professional adapting to a direct communication style abroad while keeping her own gentler manner.

passage: Sit down, Gurleen puttar, I'll tell you about Dubai. I was twenty when I went to work at the port. My supervisor was Filipino, my roommate Egyptian, the canteen man from Kerala. First month, I shook hands with a colleague's wife before she offered her hand. She stepped back. I felt like a fool. My Egyptian roommate explained, kindly, that many people there waited for the woman to offer first. I didn't know. So I learned: watch first, ask when unsure, and don't assume your home rules are the only rules. And I learned people forgive mistakes if you're respectful. My Filipino boss once came to our gurdwara for langar. He covered his head without being told. That's respect. Remember it when you go to Canada.

qa.q: Where was the narrator's supervisor from?
qa.a: The narrator's supervisor was Filipino.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel after the handshake moment?
qa.a: The narrator felt foolish and embarrassed at making a colleague's wife uncomfortable.

qa.q: What advice from the narrator could Gurleen use in Canada?
qa.a: Watch first, ask when unsure, and don't assume home customs are the only way.

qa.q: How might the Filipino boss have felt covering his head at the gurdwara?
qa.a: He probably wanted to show respect for a custom that wasn't his, and it clearly meant a lot to the narrator.

grounding: Shows an elder passing on lessons about respecting different social norms while working among many cultures.

passage: Kavitha had two hours to prepare the Bengaluru office for a video call with a new client team in Nairobi, and the conference room's internet kept dropping. Her senior, Trisha, was stuck in traffic. Kavitha had planned to open with the numbers, the way her team liked. But last week one of the Kenyan managers had spent five minutes asking about everyone's families before business. So she rewrote her opening: a warm welcome, a question about how their week had gone, then the plan. When the connection finally held, the Kenyan lead smiled and talked about his daughter's school exams. Trisha joined late, heard the relaxed tone, and messaged Kavitha: 'Nice start 👏'. They got through every agenda point anyway, just ten minutes later than planned.

qa.q: Where was the client team calling from?
qa.a: The client team was calling from Nairobi.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha change her opening?
qa.a: She remembered the Kenyan manager's warm small talk last week and wanted the client to feel respected in their own style.

qa.q: What worked about Kavitha's approach under pressure?
qa.a: She adapted quickly to the client's norms while still covering every agenda point, balancing warmth with work.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had started straight with numbers?
qa.a: The Kenyan team might have found it abrupt and felt less comfortable, which could have made the new relationship harder.

grounding: Shows a young professional adapting her communication style to another culture's norms under time pressure.

passage: In her first week at a design studio in Coimbatore, Ira kept waiting for Pema, her new teammate from Thimphu, to say whether he liked her logo drafts. He only said, 'Hmm, this one is also interesting,' and smiled. Ira, used to her old Delhi office where people said 'no, redo it' bluntly, assumed he approved. She sent the draft to the client. The next day Pema quietly showed her his own notes: three concerns he had hoped she would notice. Ira felt her face heat. That evening, over chai, she asked him how feedback worked where he grew up. 'We don't like to embarrass someone,' he said. 'But I should have been clearer.' They agreed he would write one clear concern per draft, and she would ask directly, 'What would you change?' By Friday Ira found she admired how gently he said hard things.

qa.q: Where is Pema from?
qa.a: Thimphu.

qa.q: Why did Ira's face heat when Pema showed his notes?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, realising she had read his polite 'interesting' as approval and sent the draft too soon.

qa.q: What agreement helped them work across their styles?
qa.a: Pema writes one clear concern per draft and Ira asks directly what he would change, bridging indirect and blunt habits.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt when Ira sent the draft to the client?
qa.a: Perhaps uneasy and partly responsible, since he admits he should have been clearer.

grounding: Shows two colleagues from different backgrounds adapting their feedback styles and coming to respect each other.

passage:
'Bhaiya, why do you keep saying sorry to the auto driver?' Kishore asked, dropping onto the sofa.
Ujjwal laughed. 'Habit. A year in Osaka does that.'
Papa looked up from the paper. 'And you came home at exactly seven like a train. Suddenly punctual?'
'There, if a meeting says ten, people are there before ten. My first week I strolled in at ten-fifteen, and my team lead didn't say anything, just looked at the clock. I wanted to disappear.'
'So they're strict,' Kishore said.
'Not strict exactly. Just different. People are very quiet on trains, nobody talks loudly on the phone. I learned by watching before I spoke.'
'And did you teach them anything?'
Ujjwal grinned. 'A colleague now makes chai with ginger. Badly. But he tries.'
Papa smiled. 'Good. You went respectfully and came back the same boy.'

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal spend a year?
qa.a: In Osaka.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when his team lead looked at the clock?
qa.a: Deeply embarrassed; he says he wanted to disappear.

qa.q: What approach helped Ujjwal adapt in Osaka?
qa.a: Watching before speaking, noticing norms like punctuality and quiet trains, and adjusting without judging them as strict.

qa.q: How does Papa see the change in Ujjwal?
qa.a: He is pleased that Ujjwal adapted respectfully while still coming home as the same boy 😊

grounding: A family conversation shows a young man describing how he adapted to different work and social norms abroad.
